turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Brennan. I'm Niamh. I'll get your weight and blood pressure before the doctor sees you. Shoes off if you don't mind.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Weight is eighty-nine point two kilograms. Blood pressure one thirty-eight over eighty-two. Pulse seventy-six. All grand.
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's put on a bit since Christmas, hasn't he. I'm Claire, his daughter.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come on in, the two of you. I'm Dr Keane. Sit down there. What's been the bother?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Knee.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Which knee is it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Right.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): And what's it stopping you doing?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Stairs.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): Going down the stairs, more than coming up?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Down.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does it catch you at night as well?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Night.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The right knee, going down the stairs, and it wakes him at night.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long has the pain on the stairs been going on?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Year.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Ah Dad, it's not a year. It's about three months, since the cold came in.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between three months and a year. We won't fall out over it. Can either of you say when the night pain started?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Dunno.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I couldn't put a day on the night-time bit either.
[SEG0022] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's alright. How bad is it on a day the stairs are against you?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Bad.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): Does the knee swell up on you at all?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0026] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's a maybe, so I won't write swelling down as a fact. Any locking, or does it give way under you?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or is the knee hot and red?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): And shortness of breath, or chest pain, while we're at it?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been using the diclofenac gel from the chemist, the one percent, on the right knee.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Are you putting that on twice a day, the way the box says?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll take that as a maybe. And the diclofenac tablets for the knee, from the chemist, now and again?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0037] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to stick my head in. The chart I have says diclofenac fifty milligrams, when required.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That's not right. The box at home is seventy-five milligrams. He takes the seventy-fives.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): Grand, we'll leave the dose unsettled rather than guess. Any stomach trouble with those tablets?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you live with Claire?
[SEG0042] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does, with myself and Tom, the last two years.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Lovely. Before we go on, did you catch the hurling at the weekend? My lot were hopeless.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Don't start me. We were stuck on the M50 an hour, rain belting down, trying to get to the grandchild's match, and the small lad's team lost by a point. Pure drama.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Rain.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Typical Irish summer. I watched the puddles and missed the score. Anyway, back to yourself.

[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pain going down the stairs and at night can be the joint surface, a bit of cartilage, the kneecap, or plain wear and tear. I'm not putting a name on it today, and I won't say it's coming from the hip. Not till I've had a proper look.
[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right knee now. It's not hot. There's crepitus when I bend it. No swelling that I can see. Bending is a small bit short of full.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): You said the stomach was grand. What about heartburn, acid coming up?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Heartburn.
[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He had it two nights ago after the tablet. He never said it the first time.

[SEG0052] person_4 (DOCTOR): So the heartburn is there. I'd ease off those diclofenac tablets. Paracetamol is kinder on the stomach if you need a painkiller. And eighty-nine kilos is a fair load on that step, so bringing the weight down would help the knee.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): We could send you to the physio, or we could do a steroid injection into the knee. I'm not deciding that for you today. Have a think with Claire.
[SEG0054] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll talk it over at home. He hates the idea of a needle, but the stairs are the real problem.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): If the pain is no better in six weeks, come back to me and we'll pick one. Mind the stairs in the meantime, one step at a time.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand.

spec.situation: Older patient with knee pain going down stairs and at night; uses diclofenac gel and sometimes tablets from the pharmacy; says no stomach problems and then mentions heartburn; weight discussed; physio or injection discussed, not decided.
features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

bad.reason: Heartburn is supported, but onset/aggravation came from family member, not patient.
bad.text: heartburn (category=gastrointestinal, status=present, onset=two nights ago, temporality=current, aggravating_factors=diclofenac tablet, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

omissions.text: Negative GI side effect history was recorded wrongly/ incompletely: when specifically asked about stomach trouble from diclofenac tablets, the patient first said 'No', but on further questioning he did report heartburn/acid coming up, with the daughter adding it occurred two nights ago after the tablet. The initial denial of stomach trouble and the contradiction are clinically important to retain.

Possible knee swelling was discussed but not recorded as uncertain: the patient answered 'Mm, I suppose' when asked if the knee swells, and the doctor explicitly said he would not write swelling down as a fact.
The doctor stated he was not putting a diagnosis on the knee pain today and specifically would not say it was coming from the hip until proper examination.

Decision-making/plan detail missing: the doctor said he was not deciding between physiotherapy and a steroid injection that day and asked the patient to think it over with Claire; the family member said they would discuss it at home and that he hates the idea of a needle.
